records.text: Fork deployed! One attacker hits several targets at the same time.
Alert! A fork is now available to the other side: one of their pieces can strike several targets at a stroke. Locate that piece, first priority.
Another move had a fork primed, one attacker on several targets together. This move never gives the order.
Pinned to the king and held at its post. That piece can't leave the line without exposing its own king.
Status report: the other side has a pin to the king in reach. Once pinned, it can't leave that line without exposing the king.
Another move could have pinned a piece to its king and held it there. That piece would have been frozen at its post, unable to leave the line without exposing the king. Opportunity declined.
Skewer on target! Attack the front piece, and once it clears the line, the rear piece is exposed. Textbook.
Watch the line! A skewer opens for the other side: when the front piece moves, the piece behind it could be exposed.
Loaded skewer, sitting in a stronger move. Drive off the front piece, and the rear one is exposed. This move passes on that order.
Target the defender. Capture it, and its ward stands unprotected. Standard procedure.
Defender in the open! The other side can capture it, and whatever it guards could end up unprotected. Check its duties now.
Another move could have captured a defender and stripped the protection from what it guarded. Not this time.
Back rank, and the king's own troops are the walls. That's the mating pattern, and it works!
Back rank under threat! The other side gets a route to mate there, with the king trapped behind its own pieces.
A back-rank mate was ready, with the king hemmed in by its own troops. This move stands down instead.
The mission is promotion: a pawn reaches the last rank and earns a new rank as a piece. Track its route up the board.
Eyes on that pawn! The other side gets a shot at promotion. Track its route to the last rank.
A stronger move sent a pawn toward the last rank to promote. This move leaves it waiting in the ranks.
Discovered attack, launched! The blocker moves off, and the piece behind it goes on the attack. Two units in action off a single order.
Heads up! A discovered attack is now available to the other side. Watch for a piece of theirs stepping aside to unleash the one behind it.
Another move carried a discovered attack: step one piece aside, and the one behind it goes to work. This move doesn't give that order.
Double attack deployed! Two fronts, one order, and both demand an answer.
Two-front warning! A double attack opens for the other side, two threats at once. Find both before any reply.
Two fronts at once: that's what a stronger move had. This one stays on a single front.
Deflection executed! Draw the defender off its post, and whatever it was covering is left open.
Posts under pressure! The other side can pull a defender away with a deflection, and what it guards could be left open.
There was a defender to draw off its post in another move. That deflection never gets ordered.
Unguarded piece, captured. No defender, no problem. Target collected.
Another move could have captured an undefended piece, and this one goes right past it. Sweep for unguarded pieces first.
Sentry missing! A piece stands with no defender, and the other side can take it.
Hold the post! This move pulls a piece's only effective defender off duty, and the other side can take what it was guarding.
Unanswered threat! The opponent's last move set it up, and now a piece can be captured. Every threat gets an answer.
Full count on that exchange! This capture lets the other side recapture something worth more. That trade costs the mover.
Minor piece deployed off the back rank. Another unit on duty!
Another move would have called a minor piece up from its starting square.
The rook holds an open file, cleared of every pawn. Clear road ahead.
Another move would have handed a rook an open file, empty of pawns.
The rook is posted on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns stand on it, but at least one enemy pawn does.
With another move, a rook would have had a semi-open file: no pawns of its own color on it, at least one enemy pawn ahead.
A passed pawn on the field! The road ahead is free of enemy pawns, on its own file and either neighbor. Note it on the map.
Another move had a passed pawn on offer, with no enemy pawns ahead on its file or either flank.
Forward march! The passed pawn was already free, and now it's one square closer.
Another move would have sent the passed pawn on another advance.
Isolation: a pawn with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. No backup on its flanks.
Another move would have cut a pawn off from support on both flanks: isolated.
Reinforcements! A piece with no guard just got one.
Another move would have sent a defender to a piece that had none.
No guard on this piece now. That alone doesn't mean it can be won, but keep watch.
Another move would have stripped a piece of its defender, which alone wouldn't mean it could be won.
New exit for the king, a legal square it lacked a move ago. Always worth having.
Another move would have given the king a fresh exit.
Castling complete! The king and rook both move in a single turn. Formation set.
The alternative was castling, which moves king and rook together in one turn.
One capture, and that bishop pair is finished. The side that lost the bishop no longer has one on each square color.
Another move would have taken a bishop and split the opposing bishop pair.
Doubled pawns on the field: same color, same file, one in front of the other.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, one stacked ahead of the other on a single file.
Priority alert. This move leaves the king open to a forced checkmate. Retrace the attack and find where the defense broke.
Forced checkmate was available, and this move stands down. Back to that position. Find the finish.
Sacrifice on the board, and it holds. Even accepted, the sacrifice survives the line we checked.
Last line of defense. This was the lone move we checked that stayed playable; every other choice lost.
Only this move kept the advantage among the ones we checked; all the others lost. Mission-critical.
Incoming! An immediate capture is waiting for the other side. Inspect that reply first.
Incoming check: that's the strongest reply. The king gets defended before anything else.
The engine has a different move at the top of its orders. Set it up and compare the replies.
This costs value next to the engine's best. Check the reply and see what gave way.
Engine report: strong, very little value left behind.
Sound move, solid footing. The engine's first choice is elsewhere, but this keeps most of the position's value.
The human-move model calls this natural, and the engine finds a stronger move. Tempting is not the same as correct.
Unexpected, the human-move model reports; the engine's verdict is strong. Approved.
There was one defense that kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
The engine's best, and the human-move model and the other searched moves say it was hard to find. Commit that one to memory.
Held! The position survives as playable, and the human-move model and the searched alternatives rate it a hard defense to find.
Natural by the human-move model's count and first on the engine's list. Green light!
Human-move model on this one: natural. Engine: strong, with a different move in first place.
Low on time before this move. Decisions on a short clock still count.
Fast decision, with time still on the clock.
This move got a long briefing on the clock.
Opening move on record. Standard drill.
End of the manual: the game leaves our opening book here. From now on, it's open country.
Back in the fight! Playable again, and this move did it after the earlier setback.
The setback is repaired, with help from the other side's errors. Take the reinforcements.
Chance seized! The opponent's last move offered an opening, and this move went straight for it.
The opponent's last move offered a chance, and this move overlooks it. Back to that moment for the right response.
Same issue, earlier in this game. Line those moments up and find the common weak spot.
Support restored! That piece left unguarded earlier is back under guard.
Another small concession logged. Together with the earlier ones, they've worn the position down. Review the whole sequence.
The edge was held through to the win! Review that stretch and see how it was done.
The same issue shows up in other saved games. Put them on the study list together.
Checkmate, mission complete! The king is surrounded, with no legal way out.
Checkmate, and the king is boxed in. Regroup and find where the defense could have held.
Draw declared. The result stands, but the earlier decisions still deserve an inspection.
Survey the board, then make your move when ready.
Negative. Reset and try another move.
That attempt didn't report back. Run it again.
Saved engine analysis reports a forced checkmate for the side that played this move.
Saved engine analysis flags a forced checkmate for the other side once this move is played.
At the end of the saved line, the side that played this move is ahead on material compared with the start.
At the end of the saved line, the side that played this move is behind on material compared with the start.
Clearance granted for this exercise. The moves shown don't reveal a clear tactical reason, and none is invented here.
Not cleared for this exercise. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves, so try another.
Match confirmed: the move is on this exercise's saved list. Those saved answers set what passes.
Not on this exercise's saved-answer list. Off the list doesn't mean off the mark: another legal move can still be reasonable.
Inspect the move. Next position after that.
Top work! The reason behind it goes in the kit too.
Practice logged, schedule untouched.
Solved, and logged. This one stays on the relearning list.
Starting position, before any moves.
Next move up. Note what changes.
Check on the king! That gets dealt with first.
The king gets clear of check.
Promoted! The pawn earns its new rank on the last row.
Promotion on the last rank, with check.
The pawn promotes on the last rank with checkmate. The king is boxed in for good.
Promotion on the last rank, and the promoting side's king is out of check.
Capture made. One piece leaves the board.
Capture, plus check.
A capture that's also checkmate. Every escape route is closed.
A capture, and check is lifted from the king.
Capture and promotion on the last rank, all in one move.
One pawn captures, promotes on the last rank and gives check. Busy soldier!
One pawn captures, promotes and mates. Every square around that king is denied.
A pawn capture on the last rank brings promotion, and its king is out of check too.
Castling, and the rook gives check on arrival.
Castling delivers checkmate, and the king is cut off from every legal square.
One attacker hits several targets, then takes one. This example also ends with a material gain for that side.
That piece can't capture. The pin to its king holds it: leave the line, and the king is exposed.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece has no free retreat, so any escape has to keep the king shielded.
The defenders are pinned to their king and can't recapture. Capture confirmed, and the line shown gains material.
Eyes on the pinned piece. Its king would be exposed if it left the line, and these moves capture it.
Once the front piece gets out of the way, the piece behind it is captured on the same line.
Check pushes the king aside, and then the attacker claims what stood behind.
The lone defender is taken out first, and its charge follows.
The defender is lured off its post, and its abandoned piece is captured.
The blocker moves, the line opens, and the capture comes from the piece behind it.
A piece clears the way, and the one behind it gives check.
Double check, two checking pieces at once!
The first piece attacks and uncovers a second attacker. The capture comes from that second piece.
Promotion, and the example finishes with that side up material.
Captured: one undefended piece, and by the end of the example the capturing side is up material.
A relative pin used to hold the attacking piece. The opponent's last move ended it, the target sat still, and the line shown takes it.
The other side has the reply marked on the board. Play it and see what follows.
Before moving, inspect your pieces for any that can be captured with no useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, scan for undefended enemy pieces.
Check forcing moves for a single attacker that hits two valuable targets.
Before moving a pinned piece, check what it's guarding behind it: the king, or a bigger asset.
Past the first target, keep scanning. A line attack can hit what's standing behind.
Before trading off a defender, confirm what it's protecting.
When a blocking piece moves, see what line it opens.
Hunt for one order that opens two fronts. A check or a freshly opened line counts as a front.
Before moving a back-rank defender, secure an escape square for your king.
Count the moves to promotion, and look at which pawn pushes force a response.
A defender on the move leaves something uncovered. Check what, before it goes.
Tally both halves of the exchange: what you take, and what comes back.
Check whether a forcing exchange can pull a defender off another duty.
In this exercise, the saved answers give the orders. Moves outside them aren't automatically mistakes.
Here is one way play could go if the replies are strong. Not all of those replies are forced.
Material changes cover only the line shown, counted from its start. The written explanation names the piece values used in that count.
The saved line doesn't establish a simple tactical reason, and no positional reason is claimed. March through it and weigh every reply.
The answer policy saved for this exercise governs this explanation. Check the written notes for the setting in use.
Here are the moves of your study line, in order.
Confirmed: part of your study material.
Your move should come from the study lines you selected.
A move from any of your selected opening lines counts.
Name a move from your study material.
Wrong line: that move isn't in your selected openings. Reset and go again.
Not from your selected opening lines, so go again. The study changed, so this saved attempt doesn't affect its review schedule.
Outside your selected opening lines, so go again. This position is retired, and its review schedule stays as is.
Under mixed Due, moves from this line all count. Dedicated practice drills this line exclusively.
Scheduled recalls drill the moves of your chosen side. A position shared by your active studies uses one card.
Reload the saved session, then carry on.
Verified line, running on the board now.
Revealed, and logged that way. Solution available for replay below.
Second attempt, full solution! Miss and finish: both go in the log.
Full solution, zero wrong moves. Flawless execution!
Negative on that move for this puzzle. Everything correct so far is logged.
Affirmative! Next objective: the following move.
Work out the line first. Commit after that.
Not enough from the engine to explain this position. No guessing.
Review standing by. Hit resume below, or take a piece out on patrol.
Choose any move to inspect, or move a piece and run your own test.
Straight from the manual: a book move.
This move is in the field manual: a known opening line. Proceed.
It's in the manual, under a recognized opening line.
Still following the manual.
The manual supplies another move. Carry on.
Even the reply is straight from the manual.
The manual is still in charge. Steady.
Manual still open. Formation holds.
Still marching to the book's beat.
The drill continues: another book move.
The manual still covers it. Book status tells you where we stand, not what the move is worth.
Code red. The human-move model calls this move natural, and it allows a forced checkmate. Retrace the attack and find the breach.
The human-move model calls this natural, but a forced checkmate was on the board and this move lets it go. When mate is available, mate is the order.
Natural, per the human-move model, but a capture is waiting for the other side right away. Inspect that reply first.
The human-move model rates this natural, and the engine finds a stronger move. This one gives up value, and the reply pinpoints it.
The human-move model expects this move, and it hands the other side a fork. One of their pieces can hit several targets at once. Locate that piece.
Natural to the human-move model, but now the other side has a skewer. Once the front piece shifts, whatever stands behind could be exposed.
Held under pressure! It was the only searched move that kept the position playable, and the human-move model logs it as a hard defense to find. Line held!
Only one checked move kept the position playable, and this was it. Every other choice lost. Engine's report: best. Human-move model's report: hard to find. Top marks!
This was the one searched move that kept the advantage, and every other choice lost. The human-move model's intel marks it a hard resource to find. Outstanding!
Every other move we checked gave up the advantage and lost. This one held it. The engine ranks it first, and the human-move model and the other searched moves mark it a hard find.
Fork deployed, one attacker on several targets. Human-move model's report: unexpected. Engine's report: strong. Bold works!
One attacker, several targets, all at once: a fork. Best by the engine's ranking, and hard to spot by the human-move model's intel. Good hunting!
A pin to the king holds that piece at its post; stepping off would leave its king exposed. The human-move model never saw it coming, and the engine still passes it as strong.
That piece is pinned to its king and can't leave the line without exposing it. First on the engine's list, and the human-move model logs it as hard to find.
Hold the post! The human-move model calls this natural, but it pulls a piece's only effective defender off duty, and the other side can capture what it left.
This pulls a piece's only effective defender off duty, so the piece it guarded is now capturable. One checked move would have held, and the human-move model logs that defense as hard to find.
The opponent's last move made a threat, and this natural-looking move ignores it, so a piece can be captured. Natural, per the human-move model; unanswered, per the board.

The threat from the opponent's last move goes unanswered, and a piece can be captured. A single defense was available among the moves we checked, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
The human-move model calls this capture natural, but the recapture costs more than it takes. Tally the full trade.
This capture invites a recapture of something worth more. The only playable move we found was elsewhere, and by the human-move model's intel, it was a tough find.
Fork on the board! One attacker hits several targets. Human-move model's report: natural. Engine's report: best. Approved.
There's a fork here, one attacker hitting several targets. Human-move model's report: natural. Engine's report: strong, with a different move in first place.
Alert: the other side has a fork, one of their pieces hitting several targets at once. Exactly one checked move held the line, and the human-move model logs it as hard to see.
Another move had a fork, one attacker on several targets. The human-move model expects this move instead, and the fork never gets ordered.
The only move that held carried a fork, one piece hitting several targets. This move took another route, and the human-move model says the fork was well camouflaged.
Pinned and held: that piece can't leave the line without exposing its king. The human-move model saw it coming, and the engine ranks it first. Orders confirmed.
A pin to the king keeps that piece at its post. In the human-move model's log, it's natural. The engine rates it strong but keeps a different move in front.
The human-move model calls this natural, but it opens a pin to the king for the other side. That piece would be stuck on the line.
The other side now has a pin to the king available. One defense stood among the moves we checked, and the human-move model says it was easy to miss.
A stronger move had a pin to the king in reserve. The human-move model calls this one natural, and the pin never happens.
Only one move held, and it was a pin to the king. That order never went out, and the human-move model rates it a hard find.
Skewer in place! Drive off the front piece, and the rear piece is left exposed. The engine's top pick, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
Skewer, lined up: once the front piece moves, the rear piece is in the open. Off the human-move model's map, but the engine stamps it strong.
Skewer executed: front piece moves, rear piece exposed. Natural on the human-move model's intel, and best on the engine's. Textbook.
Two pieces on one line, and the front one has to move. Then the rear piece is exposed. Natural is the human-move model's call. The engine passes it as strong, though another move outranks it.

Skewer threat on the line for the other side: once the front piece moves, the rear piece is open to attack. One checked move would have held, and the human-move model logs that defense as hard to find.
A stronger move had a skewer, the front piece moving and the rear piece exposed. The human-move model calls this one natural, and the skewer goes unused.
The only playable move we found held a skewer, exposing the rear piece once the front one moved. It slipped away, and the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
Target the defender. Capture it, and what it guarded loses its protection. The engine puts it first, and by the human-move model's intel, it was a tough find. Outstanding work!
Capture the defender, and whatever it protected is left without cover. Unconventional by the human-move model's intel, strong by the engine's.
Defender captured, and what it covered loses its protection. Both reports agree: natural to the human-move model, best for the engine.
Defender down, and its charge loses that cover. Expected by the human-move model, passed as strong by the engine, and outranked by the engine's favorite.
Natural by the human-move model's intel, but a defender is now open to capture. If it falls, what it guards could lose protection.
A defender is now open to capture, and its charge could end up unprotected. A single defense was available among the moves we checked, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
Another move could have captured a defender and left its charge unprotected. Instead, the human-move model's expected move goes out, and that defender stays on guard.
Our only playable move was the capture of a defender, stripping its protection. Nobody gave that order, and the human-move model says it was hard to spot.
The king is walled in on the back rank by its own pieces. Engine's report: best. Human-move model's report: hard to find. Top marks!
Back rank locked down: the king's own troops wall off every exit. A surprise to the human-move model, and a strong move to the engine. Approved.
Back rank sealed: the king's own pieces block the exits. The human-move model logs it as natural, and the engine puts it at the top of the list. Approved.
There's a back-rank mating idea here, with the king boxed in by its own troops. The human-move model marks it natural, and the engine passes it as strong, with its favorite elsewhere.
A pawn on its way to the last rank to become a new piece. The engine ranks it first, and the human-move model and the other searched moves mark it a hard find.
Promotion is the mission, a pawn headed for the last rank. The human-move model logs it as unusual, and the engine logs it as strong.
Promotion in sight: a pawn marching toward the last rank. Expected by the human-move model and ranked first by the engine. Clean sweep.
Promotion is the objective, a pawn pressing for the last rank. Natural, per the human-move model's intel; strong, per the engine, which still prefers another move.
The human-move model logs this as natural, but one of their pawns now has a shot at promotion. Track it to the last rank.
This gives one of their pawns a road to promotion. The only playable move we found was elsewhere, and by the human-move model's intel, it was a tough find.
Another move would have sent a pawn to the last rank to promote. The human-move model calls this one natural, and the pawn stays in the ranks.
Our only playable move was a pawn push toward promotion. That advance never happened, and the human-move model says it was hard to find.
Discovered attack, live! One piece steps aside, and the one behind it goes on the attack. Best by the engine's ranking, and hard to spot by the human-move model's intel. Good hunting!
The blocker steps clear, opening fire for the piece behind it. Human-move model's report: unexpected. Engine's report: strong. Bold works!
The front piece moves, and the piece behind it is suddenly attacking. Human-move model's report: natural. Engine's report: best. Approved.
A blocker steps aside to uncover an attack from the piece behind it. Intel from the human-move model: natural. The engine's assessment: strong, with a different move in first place.
The human-move model calls this natural, but a discovered attack opens for the other side. One of their pieces can clear the line and unmask the attacker behind it.
A discovered attack opens for the other side: one piece steps aside to unmask another. Exactly one checked move held the line, and the human-move model logs it as hard to see.
Another move carried a discovered attack: one piece steps aside, and the one behind it opens up. This is the move the human-move model predicts, and the attack never launches.
Our only playable move was a discovered attack, one piece clearing the line for another. The order was never given, and the human-move model logs it as a hard find.
Two fronts, one order: each threat demands an answer. First on the engine's list, and the human-move model logs it as hard to find.
Double attack: two fronts opened with one move. The human-move model never saw it coming, and the engine still passes it as strong.
Two fronts opened at once: double attack on the board. The human-move model saw it coming, and the engine ranks it first. Orders confirmed.
Double attack, two fronts at once. In the human-move model's log, it's natural. The engine rates it strong but keeps a different move in front.
The human-move model calls this natural, but now the other side has a double attack. Two threats arrive together, and each needs an answer.
Double attack available to the other side now. One defense stood among the moves we checked, and the human-move model says it was easy to miss.
A different move would have opened two fronts at once. The human-move model expects this one, and the double attack never gets launched.
The only playable move we found opened two fronts at once. That attack never launched, and the human-move model says it was hard to spot.
Deflection: the defender is drawn off its post. The engine's top pick, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
Pull the defender off its post, and its post sits empty. Off the human-move model's map, but the engine stamps it strong.
Deflection, by the numbers! The defender leaves its post, and what it guarded is open. Natural on the human-move model's intel, and best on the engine's. Textbook.
A defender is drawn off its post here: deflection. Natural is the human-move model's call. The engine passes it as strong, though another move outranks it.
Natural, the human-move model reports, but the other side now has a deflection. A defender could be pulled away, leaving what it guards open.
The other side can now draw a defender off its post. One checked move would have held, and the human-move model logs that defense as hard to find.
There was a deflection in another move, pulling a defender off its post. The human-move model's pick is this one, and that defender never leaves its post.
The one playable move on record was a deflection, pulling a defender away from its post. The defender stayed put, and the human-move model rates that deflection hard to see.
Unguarded target, taken. The engine puts it first, and by the human-move model's intel, it was a tough find. Outstanding work!
No defender on that piece, and this move captures it. Unconventional by the human-move model's intel, strong by the engine's.
Unguarded piece taken. Both reports agree: natural to the human-move model, best for the engine.
Captured: a piece that had no defender. Expected by the human-move model, passed as strong by the engine, and outranked by the engine's favorite.
An unguarded piece was there for another move to capture. The human-move model expects this one, and that piece stays on the board.
Our only playable move captured an undefended piece. That capture never happened, and the human-move model says it was hard to notice.
The human-move model calls this natural, but a piece is now without a defender, and the other side can take it.
Sentry missing: a piece is undefended, and the other side can take it. A single defense was available among the moves we checked, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
From its starting square, a minor piece enters service. Engine ranking: best. Human-move model intel: hard to find. Top marks!
A minor piece leaves the barracks. A surprise to the human-move model, and a strong move to the engine.
A knight or bishop joins the action from its starting square. The human-move model logs it as natural, and the engine puts it at the top of the list.
Knight or bishop, off the starting square and onto the front line. The human-move model marks it natural, and the engine passes it as strong, with its favorite elsewhere.
Open file secured for the rook, empty of pawns. The engine ranks it first, and the human-move model and the other searched moves mark it a hard find.
The rook commands a file with no pawns of either color. The human-move model logs it as unusual, and the engine logs it as strong.
The rook holds an open file, clear of pawns. Expected by the human-move model and ranked first by the engine. Clean sweep.
Open lane for the rook, zero pawns of either color on it. Natural, per the human-move model's intel; strong, per the engine, which still prefers another move.
Rook on a semi-open file: no pawns of its own color on it, at least one enemy pawn ahead. Best by the engine's ranking, and hard to spot by the human-move model's intel. Good hunting!
A semi-open file for the rook, with an enemy pawn on it and none of its own. Logged by the human-move model as unexpected; cleared as strong by the engine. Bold works!
The rook is on a semi-open file, enemy pawns only. Briefing: natural for the human-move model for the human-move model, and the engine's orders read best.
Semi-open file under the rook's command, with no pawns of its own color on it. Field notes: intel says natural, and the engine's ranking says strong, with a different move in first place.
Passed pawn on the map, with the road clear of enemy pawns on its file and the files beside it. First on the engine's list, and the human-move model logs it as hard to find.
Passed pawn on the board, with the path ahead clear of enemy pawns on its file and both neighbors. The human-move model never saw it coming, and the engine still passes it as strong.
A new passed pawn, clear of enemy pawns ahead on its file and both neighbors. The human-move model saw it coming, and the engine ranks it first. Orders confirmed.
Here's a new passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or the neighboring ones. In the human-move model's log, it's natural. The engine rates it strong but keeps a different move in front.
Forward march: another square for the passed pawn. The engine's top pick, and the human-move model says it was well camouflaged.
The passed pawn takes another square of ground. Off the human-move model's map, but the engine stamps it strong.
Advance continues for the passed pawn. Natural on the human-move model's intel, and best on the engine's. Textbook.
The passed pawn gains ground once more. Natural is the human-move model's call. The engine passes it as strong, though another move outranks it.
Isolated pawn, with no friendly pawn on either flank. The engine puts it first, and by the human-move model's intel, it was a tough find. Outstanding work!
An isolated pawn remains, no backup on either neighboring file. Unconventional by the human-move model's intel, strong by the engine's.
One pawn is left isolated, no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. Both reports agree: natural to the human-move model, best for the engine. Sometimes a weakness is an acceptable cost.
A pawn ends up isolated, no friendly pawn on either flank. Expected by the human-move model, passed as strong by the engine, and outranked by the engine's favorite.
